items.sentence_raw: Tourism, holidaymaking and travel are these days more significant social phenomena than most commentators have considered.
On the face of it there could not be a more trivial subject for a book.
items.explain: Q33: The passage says *'On the face of it there could not be a more trivial subject for a book'* — **'on the face of it'** means this is how it first appears, not the real truth. The writer then argues tourism is actually important. So the statement 'Tourism is a trivial subject' is what the writer disagrees with — the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: And indeed since social scientists have had considerable difficulty explaining weightier topics, such as work or politics, it might be thought that they would have great difficulties in accounting for more trivial phenomena such as holidaymaking.
However, there are interesting parallels with the study of deviance.

Then it says *'there are interesting parallels with the study of deviance'* and that a *'similar analysis can be applied to tourism'*. This means the writer is **justifying** why we should study tourism. So the heading is **iii** — **Justifying the study of tourism**.

items.sentence_raw: Tourism is a leisure activity which presupposes its opposite, namely regulated and organised work.
items.explain:
Q29: The passage says tourism *'presupposes its opposite, namely regulated and organised work'* and is a *'defining characteristic of being modern'*. This shows tourism is a key part of modern life — its **essence**. So the heading is **v** — **The essence of modern tourism**.

Q38: The passage says tourism *'presupposes its opposite, namely regulated and organised work'* and shows how work and leisure are *'separate and regulated spheres'*. This **distinction** between work and leisure is what creates the idea of tourism. So the answer is **D** — **the distinction we make between work and leisure**.

items.sentence_raw: It is one manifestation of how work and leisure are organised as separate and regulated spheres of social practice in modern societies.

items.sentence_raw: Indeed acting as a tourist is one of the defining characteristics of being 'modern' and the popular concept of tourism is that it is organised within particular places and occurs for regularised periods of time.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says tourism *'presupposes its opposite, namely regulated and organised work'* and is a *'defining characteristic of being modern'*. This shows tourism is a key part of modern life — its **essence**. So the heading is **v** — **The essence of modern tourism**.

items.sentence_raw: Tourist relationships arise from a movement of people to, and their stay in, various destinations.
This necessarily involves some movement, that is the journey, and a period of stay in a new place or places.

'The journey and the stay' are by definition outside the normal places of residence and work and are of a short term and temporary nature and there is a clear intention to return 'home' within a relatively short period of time.

A substantial proportion of the population of modern societies engages in such tourist practices new socialised forms of provision have developed in order to cope with the mass character of the gazes of tourists as opposed to the individual character of travel.
items.explain: Q30: The passage contrasts the *'mass character of the gazes of tourists'* with the *'individual character of travel'*. This directly shows tourism is different from travel — it is a **contrast**. So the heading is **iv** — **Tourism contrasted with travel**.

items.sentence_raw: Places are chosen to be visited and be gazed upon because there is an anticipation especially through daydreaming and fantasy of intense pleasures, either on a different scale or involving different senses from those customarily encountered.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says *'anticipation is constructed and sustained through... films, TV literature, magazines'* — these are all **media**. This anticipation is about the pleasures tourists expect, so media enhances their **expectations**. So the answer is **B** — **the expectations of tourists**.

items.sentence_raw: Such anticipation is constructed and sustained through a variety of non-tourist practices such as films, TV literature, magazines records and videos which construct and reinforce this daydreaming.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says *'anticipation is constructed and sustained through... films, TV literature, magazines'* — these are all **media**. This anticipation is about the pleasures tourists expect, so media enhances their **expectations**. So the answer is **B** — **the expectations of tourists**.

items.sentence_raw: Tourists tend to visit features of landscape and townscape which separate them off from everyday experience.
Such aspects are viewed because they are taken to be in some sense out of the ordinary.

The viewing of these tourist sights often involves different forms of social patterning with a much greater sensitivity to visual elements of landscape or townscape than is normally found in everyday life.
items.explain:
Q36: The passage says tourists view sights with *'much greater sensitivity to visual elements... than is normally found in everyday life'*. This means they focus **more** on tourist places than on places at home. So the answer is **YES**.

Q40: The passage says tourists view sights with *'much greater sensitivity... than is normally found in everyday life'*. This means they look at tourist places **differently** from how they look at places in their normal daily life. So the answer is **F** — **places seen in everyday life**.

items.sentence_raw: People linger over these sights in a way that they would not normally do in their home environment and the vision is objectified or captured through photographs postcards films and so on which enable the memory to be endlessly reproduced and recaptured.
One of the earliest dissertations on the subject of tourism is Boorstins analysis of the pseudo event (1964) where he argues that contemporary.
Americans cannot experience reality directly but thrive on pseudo events.

Isolated from the host environment and the local people the mass tourist travels in guided groups and finds pleasure in inauthentic contrived attractions gullibly enjoying the pseudo events and disregarding the real world outside.
items.explain:
Q31: The passage says tourists enjoy *'inauthentic contrived attractions'* and *'pseudo events'* — **'inauthentic'** and **'contrived'** both mean **artificial**, not real. This shows modern tourism is fake. So the heading is **vii** — **The artificiality of modern tourism**.

Q41: The passage says group tourists find pleasure in *'inauthentic contrived attractions'* — **'contrived'** means specially made, and **'attractions'** are sights. These are sights designed for tourists, not real local life. So the answer is **H** — **sights designed specially for tourists**.

items.sentence_raw: Over time the images generated of different tourist sights come to constitute a closed self-perpetuating system of illusions which provide the tourist with the basis for selecting and evaluating potential places to visit.
Such visits are made says Boorstin, within the environmental bubble of the familiar American style hotel which insulates the tourist from the strangeness of the host environment.
To service the burgeoning tourist industry, an array of professionals has developed who attempt to reproduce ever-new objects for the tourist to look at.
These objects or places are located in a complex and changing hierarchy.

This depends upon the interplay between, on the one hand, competition between interests involved in the provision of such objects and, on the other hand changing class, gender, and generational distinctions of taste within the potential population of visitors.
It has been said that to be a tourist is one of the characteristics of the modern experience.
Not to go away is like not possessing a car or a nice house.
Travel is a marker of status in modern societies and is also thought to be necessary for good health.
The role of the professional, therefore, is to cater for the needs and tastes of the tourists in accordance with their class and overall expectations.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says *'the role of the professional, therefore, is to cater for the needs and tastes of the tourists'*. **'Cater for'** means to serve or guide — this is exactly what tour guides do. So the heading is **viii** — **The role of modern tour guides**.

orphan_explain_map.35: Q35: The passage talks about tourists choosing places based on daydreaming and media, but it never mentions whether they choose **overseas** or local destinations. ***The location of travel is simply not discussed***. Since the passage neither confirms nor denies this, the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
orphan_explain_map.37: Q37: The passage describes what tour professionals do — they *'cater for the needs and tastes of the tourists'* — but it never says they try to **cheat** tourists. ***'Cater for' does not mean 'cheat'***. Since there is no information about cheating, the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
